 Here’s the latest. 
 The Democratic representative who lost a primary fight against Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, appeared on Sunday with his Republican opponent, deepening an extraordinary intraparty rift two days before the midterm elections.
 The appearance by Representative Haley Stevens at a church service in Detroit with Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee, risked imperiling Democratic hopes to hold onto the Michigan seat as they seek to flip control of the Senate on Tuesday. Abby Ronson, a spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers’s campaign, posted an image of the two standing side-by-side at the service.
 The Michigan race has become a source of discomfort for Democrats in the final days of a campaign season that has otherwise put Republicans on defense, trying to stave off Democratic advances in deeply conservative corners of the country. President Trump was scheduled to travel on Sunday to Iowa and Kansas, two conservative states that have turned into Senate battlegrounds.
 Nationally, the Senate battle is a tossup, but strategists in both parties say Democrats are in a strong position to reclaim the House. The party that holds the White House typically loses seats in Congress in midterm elections.
 Republicans have been weighed down by high prices and Mr. Trump’s unpopularity but are trying to exploit the Democratic infighting to flip the Senate seat in Michigan.
 Dr. El-Sayed was attending a church service in Detroit that was intended to be a unity gathering with Ms. Stevens, whom he narrowly defeated in the primary in August, in an effort to move past her recent criticisms of him . But that plan fell apart this weekend, with Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed publicly feuding over U.S. policy on Israel.
 On Saturday, Dr. El-Sayed urged Ms. Stevens to stay away from the event, while an adviser to Representative James E. Clyburn — a South Carolina Democrat who was taking part in the event — said Ms. Stevens was still welcome.
 Just before Dr. El-Sayed took the stage, Ms. Stevens showed up at Perfecting Church in Detroit with Mr. Rogers.
 The messy fight between Democrats escalated hours before Mr. Trump was scheduled to speak in Dubuque, Iowa, in the afternoon, before a rally in Salina, Kan. He won both states by double digits in 2024, but elevated gasoline, diesel and fertilizer prices, which were driven up by the Iran war, have rattled their agriculture-heavy economies.
 Democrats believe they have a chance to ride voters’ economic discontent to Senate victories in both states. In Iowa, Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican, faces Josh Turek, a Democratic state lawmaker. In Kansas, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, is trying to fend off the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a centrist Democrat.
 Mr. Trump, who spent Saturday holding tele-rallies in Florida, shrugged off the political headwinds facing his party, telling reporters that “the country has never done better.”
 Here’s what else we’re covering:
 Wealth tax: California voters are considering a proposition that would charge a one-time, 5 percent tax on the wealth of residents worth more than $1.1 billion. At stake is a potential revolution in U.S. taxation. Read more › 
 TV ads: Almost half the political spending in the midterm elections has been directed toward local television. Though broadcast TV may not be what it once was, some consultants still see it as a key to reaching voters. The election may show whether that calculus is shifting. Read more › 
 New England power broker: Senator Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, is facing a difficult path to re-election. Her political career has been a lesson in the accrual and use of power. Read more ›

 Reporting from Michigan Representative Haley Stevens and Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, have been watching the church service from the second pew. Stevens occasionally raised her right arm in praise and seemed into the sermon, while Rogers nodded along while sharing whispers with his wife, who sat next to him. Stevens’s fiancé, Jason Turkish, also attended. 
 The service is wrapping up, and the two couples have joined the rest of the parishioners in standing and applauding the minister’s big finish. There was no reference to Stevens and Rogers during the sermon. 
 Nov. 1, 2026, 12:06 p.m. ET Bayliss Wagner and Tim Balk 
 El-Sayed’s primary opponent appears with his Senate rival. 
 Image Representative Haley Stevens, Democrat of Michigan, at an event in August. Credit... Nic Antaya for The New York Times Representative Haley Stevens, a Michigan Democrat who has been feuding with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, her party’s nominee for Senate, appeared on Sunday with his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, dramatically escalating an intraparty battle on the eve of a pivotal election.
 Ms. Stevens and Mr. Rogers attended a service at Perfecting Church in Detroit, a prominent Black church, Mr. Rogers’ campaign confirmed Sunday morning. Abby Ronson, a spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers’s campaign, posted an image of the two standing side-by-side at the service.
 It was not immediately clear whether Ms. Stevens was defecting to support Mr. Rogers in the Senate race. She previously endorsed Dr. El-Sayed.
 The appearance followed days of mounting tension between Dr. El-Sayed, a progressive and a forceful critic of Israel, and Ms. Stevens, a centrist and a supporter of Israel. Ms. Stevens had immediately threw her support to Dr. El-Sayed after he defeated her by less than a percentage point in a bitter Senate primary in August.
 But since then, their relationship has grown ever more contentious.
 Tensions mounted last week with Ms. Stevens demanding that Dr. El-Sayed denounce an ad from an outside group that she has argued amounts to “fear-mongering about Israel.” But they appeared to ease on Thursday, when Ms. Stevens said that she planned to campaign with Dr. El-Sayed this weekend.
 Those plans, however, were upended when she issued a statement Friday morning demanding an apology for comments Dr. El-Sayed had made criticizing Israel.
 Dr. El-Sayed said Saturday that he did not want Ms. Stevens to join him at a party unity event in Detroit on Sunday.
 “I don’t want any distractions,” Dr. El-Sayed told reporters Saturday. He added, “It seems as though other folks are more interested in making this race about things that it’s not about.”

 Neither Rogers nor Stevens is expected to address worshippers, who have filled nearly every one of the 3,000 or so seats in the sanctuary.

Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, a Democrat, told CBS’s “Face the Nation” that the Trump administration hadn’t provided any evidence that there were illegal immigrants on the state’s voter rolls, after the Justice Department charged four people in Pennsylvania with election crimes last week. “We take that very, very seriously, and the Trump administration has never provided a shred of evidence to suggest that there are people on our rolls who are ineligible,” Shapiro said. “If they have it. I want it, and we will act on it immediately.”
 He added that Pennsylvania’s secretary of state, a Republican he appointed to oversees the state’s election, “has done more to root out corruption than anything that’s ever been done in the Trump administration.”
 Shapiro has long pushed back against the Trump administration’s attempts to insert the federal government in state-run elections, including by successfully suing to block President Trump’s attempt to curtail mail voting.

 Reporting on campaign finance A new super PAC that seems intent on promoting spoiler candidates has now spent about $4 million over the last week, according to new filings. The group, called Our Heritage Matters and which was incorporated on Oct. 15, has primarily been backing long-shot Libertarian and third-party candidates, which could help the Democratic Party in tight races by peeling away conservative voters.
 For example, the group disclosed yesterday spending for Mark Hackett, the Constitution Party candidate in South Carolina’s Senate race, and David Graham, the Libertarian Party choice in Kansas’s Senate race.
 Nov. 1, 2026, 10:47 a.m. ET Sasha von Oldershausen 
 Reporting from Austin, Texas
 Paxton and Talarico battle over ‘what makes a Texan.’ 
 Ken Paxton speaking in McAllen, Texas, in July and James Talarico in Dallas, in October. Christopher Lee for The New York Times, Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images A Mexican ballad played across Spanish-language radio stations in Texas earlier this month. Accompanied by an upbeat guitar, a singer celebrated a young man raised by a single mother who instilled strong values:
 He’s an ally of the people 
 He’ll stand with them 
 Paxton only looks at his ambition 
 The hero of this corrido , a traditional Mexican narrative ballad, was James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas. The song was an ad commissioned by Lone Star Rising, a super PAC backing Mr. Talarico, and it was performed by Latin Grammy winner Salvador “Chava” Chavez.
 In the race for Senate, Texas culture has become its own battleground.
 From cowboy boots to a “Friday Night Lights”-inspired bus tour and an appearance at a Kacey Musgraves concert, Mr. Talarico has embraced familiar Texas touchstones on the campaign trail. His Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, has drawn on the oil industry, conservative values and cowboy mythology.
 Mr. Paxton has leaned heavily on traditional imagery of Texas.
 One advertisement celebrates the state’s oil and beef industries, accompanied by images of pump jacks and cowboys on horseback. Other ads have attacked Mr. Talarico over his past comments about reducing meat consumption and his positions on gender identity, presenting him as a candidate whose values are fundamentally at odds with those of Texas.
 The cultural shorthand is clear. Mr. Paxton’s Texas is a place of oil fields, cattle ranches and traditional values, a state whose identity is something to be defended against change.
 Both he and Mr. Talarico are making a case not just for how Texas should be governed, but for what it means to be Texan.
 “James Talarico belongs in California, not Texas,” Mr. Paxton wrote on X earlier this month, echoing attacks on the campaign trail that have cast the eighth-generation Texan as out of step with his home state.
 But it was Mr. Paxton who spent part of his childhood in California, where his father was stationed with the United States Air Force, a point that Mr. Talarico has seized upon.
 “I believe anyone can be a Texan,” Mr. Talarico said at an October rally in Plano. “It doesn’t matter if you’re an eighth-generation Texan like me, or a California transplant like Ken Paxton.”
 He added, “What makes a Texan is not in the boots or in the truck; it is deep in the heart.”
 Image A supporter of Mr. Talarico stop outside of Round Rock Donuts in Round Rock, Texas. Credit... Tamir Kalifa for The New York Times Nevertheless, Mr. Talarico has made a point of flexing his Texas bona fides: He is rarely seen without his Lucchese cowboy boots and drives a Chevrolet Colorado pickup with a bumper sticker that says “Less Honkin’ More Tonkin.’”
 His campaign tour, “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts” is a reference to the beloved TV series “Friday Night Lights,” which immortalized small-town Texas football. And after a nearly 10-day absence last month that he attributed to the flu, he made his first public reappearance at Austin City Limits, the city’s signature music festival.
 “Texas is a very proud state,” said Sharon Jarvis, a political communication researcher at the University of Texas at Austin. “You can see just how proud they are, how important these symbols are, and the rhetorical work that these symbols do.”
 Earlier this year, during a surprise appearance with Barack Obama, Mr. Talarico’s seemingly innocuous taco order — potato, egg, and cheese — sent the internet into a tailspin. Mr. Talarico has also made appearances at a Whataburger, the state’s most loved fast-food chain.
 Mr. Paxton’s supporters, meanwhile, have drawn upon a different set of cultural references, invoking the Alamo and the state’s frontier mythology to challenge Mr. Talarico’s Texas credentials.
 Image Former President Barack Obama and Mr. Talarico dropped into an Austin taco joint in May. Credit... Pool photo by Joel Angel Juarez At one October rally, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick recited lyrics from a Marty Robbins song about the Alamo, summoning one of the state’s most enduring symbols of sacrifice and independence. Mayes Middleton, a Republican state senator, took aim at Mr. Talarico’s cowboy boots, accused him of wearing a zip-up pair. They were not.
 In Texas, where the distinctions between Wranglers and Levi’s jeans, or the amount of dirt on one’s boots (Mr. Paxton also wears Luccheses), function as subtle cues of cultural legitimacy, even the smallest decisions can become politically fraught.
 Take “The Great Tamale Incident.”
 In 1976, President Gerald Ford, campaigning for re-election, stopped at the Alamo in San Antonio, where he was offered a plate of tamales. He proceeded to bite into it without removing the corn husk, a culinary faux pas that would come to haunt him.
 Image Samual Hall celebrates after Mr. Paxton wins the Republican nomination for U.S. Senate in May in Plano, Texas. Credit... Desiree Rios for The New York Times Mr. Talarico, by contrast, has sought to make room for a more expansive definition of Texas identity.
 “We’re this big mash-up of all these different people, all these different cultures, all these different friends,” he said during his stump speech in Plano earlier this month. “Think about Tejano music. If you’re listening to a Selena song, you’re hearing Spanish vocal styles from Northern Mexico, but you’re also hearing polka dance rhythms from Czech and German immigrants.”
 In a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in nearly four decades, these cultural touchstones may serve yet another function: to make the prospect of Democratic representation feel a little more familiar.
 Jesus Jiménez and Lauren McGaughy contributed reporting.

 Politics reporter On CNN’s “State of the Union,” Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Alaska Republican in a competitive re-election battle, said he would accept the election results in his race against Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee whose campaign was involved in recruiting a spoiler candidate, per reporting from The New York Times last week. 
 At President Trump’s behest, the Department of Justice asked a court to block certification of the results if Sullivan were to lose narrowly, arguing that confusion over the similarly-named candidates could taint the results.
 Sullivan also said he did not know whether or not Peltola’s campaign broke the law when it helped recruit a man named Dan J. Sullivan to run as a Republican against him. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, ordered an investigation into whether Peltola’s campaign engaged in criminal activity earlier this week.
 Nov. 1, 2026, 8:00 a.m. ET Evan Gorelick 
 A Social Security email praising Trump may violate an anticorruption law, experts say. 
 Image The Social Security Administration called itself a “model of excellence” under President Trump in an email sent to people with online accounts. Credit... Andrew Harnik/Getty Images The Social Security Administration and the Internal Revenue Service praised President Trump in mass emails sent Thursday, Friday and Saturday to people with online accounts, an unusual move days before the midterm elections that some experts said could violate federal ethics laws.
 “Under President Donald J. Trump, the Social Security Administration (SSA) is transforming into a model of excellence, one that meets and exceeds customer expectations for fast, accurate and secure service,” Frank Bisignano, the Social Security Agency’s commissioner, wrote in one of the emails, copies of which were reviewed by The New York Times.
 Mr. Bisignano, who also serves as the chief executive of the I.R.S., signed his name on a similar email sent out by the I.R.S. on Thursday, copies of which were also reviewed by The Times.
 “Last year, President Donald J. Trump signed into law the Working Families Tax Cuts, landmark legislation that ushered in a new era of tax relief and prevented the largest tax increase in American history from taking effect,” Mr. Bisignano wrote in the other email, continuing, “Hardworking Americans like you are keeping more of what they earn because of President Trump’s historic tax cuts.”
 The I.R.S. email says that it is “for informational purposes and does not constitute a communication about a taxpayer’s specific situation,” adding that the I.R.S. “does not generally send e-mails to taxpayers.”
 Several legal experts said the emails’ praise of Mr. Trump, coupled with their timing just days before a pivotal election, potentially violated the Hatch Act , an 87-year-old law meant to prevent employees of the executive branch from using their positions to influence the results of partisan elections.
 Kathleen Clark, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis, said the emails seemed to function as “propaganda” rather than as public service announcements providing practical information.
 “They’re doing it just before the election to persuade people that President Trump is doing a good job,” Richard W. Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and former White House ethics lawyer under President George W. Bush, said in a phone interview on Saturday, adding that he thought the emails were inappropriate.
 Ms. Clark said the messages were reminiscent of a television ad campaign by the Trump administration this fall that promoted his presidency. Some experts said the campaign could have violated the Hatch Act and additional statutory prohibitions on the use of appropriated funds for publicity or propaganda.
 The Social Security Administration and the I.R.S. did not respond to requests for comment.

 The Peltola campaign may have bolstered critics of Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system. 
 Image The effort by Democrats to stack Alaska’s ballot and help Mary Peltola’s Senate bid could bolster a referendum to scrap ranked-choice voting. Credit... Kerry Tasker/Reuters Organizers of a ballot measure that would end Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system say the effort by Democrats to boost Mary Peltola’s Senate bid by stacking Tuesday’s ballots in an attempt to confuse voters should be the system’s death knell.
 Since Alaska voters approved open primaries and ranked-choice general elections in 2020, opponents — most of them Republicans — have argued the system is too confusing for the average person.Now it’s been tainted by scandal involving the recruitment of a challenger with the same name as the incumbent. That has led to federal legal action, a Justice Department investigation and a separate state investigation.
 There have been similar attempts to fool the electorate with same-name candidates under other election systems in Alaska and elsewhere.
 “I mean, there it is,” said Judy Eledge, a longtime conservative activist in Alaska and chairwoman of the campaign for Ballot Measure 2, the effort to repeal Alaska’s current electoral system that voters will decide next week alongside the race for U.S. Senate. “They’ve done our work for us.”
 A similar referendum two years ago lost by 737 votes. Backers of the system still say it encourages bipartisanship and gives voters an extra layer of protection against dirty tricks and bogus candidates by offering multiple choices.
 “This situation is actually an object lesson in why you need ranked choice voting: You can’t have a spoiler when voters have multiple options,” said Joelle Hall, a longtime labor leader working against Ballot Measure 2.
 But that argument got much more difficult to make after The New York Times reported a successful effort by Democrats to recruit a candidate named Dan Sullivan to appear on the ballot alongside Senator Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican whom Ms. Peltola, a former Democratic House member, hopes to defeat.
 Besides Ms. Peltola and the two Sullivans, another name is on the ballot, Gerald Heikes, a conservative Republican and frequent candidate who said he too was recruited to run for the Senate by an outsider. A liberal political action committee is promoting Mr. Heikes in hopes of siphoning still more votes from the incumbent.
 So two of the four choices may be on the ballot because of skulduggery.
 Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a conservative Republican leaving office in December, told Fox News this week that “we wouldn’t be having this conversation if we didn’t have ranked choice voting.”
 Under current law, candidates for state and federal office in Alaska compete in one open, nonpartisan primary, with the top four advancing to November. Voters rank them in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-choice votes, the last-place finisher is eliminated and those votes are redistributed according to voters’ next choices. The process repeats until someone wins a majority of the remaining votes.
 Ballot Measure 2 would return Alaska to primaries open only to voters registered to a particular party. That would be followed by a traditional general election where voters choose just one candidate. The initiative would also repeal campaign-finance disclosure requirements adopted with the current system. Proponents of the current system have made the loss of that transparency the heart of their argument to voters.
 Even before the controversy over the two Dan Sullivans, the ballot measure was emerging as a proxy fight in a broader national battle over how America votes. Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, and Jeff Yass, a billionaire, donated heavily to the repeal effort, while Michael Bloomberg, Marc Merrill and Kathryn Murdoch, themselves deep-pocketed donors, backed the campaign to keep the system.
 Image The campaign around ranked-choice voting has attracted billionaire outsiders like Elon Musk who have turned the referendum into a showdown over how Americans should vote. Credit... Ruth Fremson/The New York Times The Times investigation has put proponents for the ranked-choice system in the awkward position of arguing that this kind of attempt to mislead could happen under any voting system because it’s comparatively easy for people to file to run in Alaska.
 “This has nothing to do with ranked-choice voting,” said Scott Kendall, an Anchorage lawyer who designed the system. “It’s just a dirty trick.”
 Ms. Peltola’s effort to unseat Senator Sullivan is critical to Democratic hopes of retaking the chamber. In response to the allegations of chicanery, Vice President JD Vance told reporters Thursday, “It seems to me that you have an election, the person who wins the most votes should win.”
 President Trump said on a Kansas City radio broadcast, “You need about a 190 I.Q.” to understand the system,” though each ballot has fairly simple instructions and the state elections division, overseen by a Republican lieutenant governor, took pains to differentiate the candidates: Dan S. Sullivan is identified on the ballot as the incumbent and a registered Republican, while Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has no identification next to his name.
 Proponents of ranked-choice voting say it just gives voters more than one chance to decide who they support — and a simple solution, supporters note, to any confusion about which Dan is which: Rank them both.
 Alaskans who rank Daniel J. Sullivan or Mr. Heikes first could still help Senator Dan S. Sullivan win, provided they also rank him ahead of Ms. Peltola. Only if they rank Ms. Peltola higher, or leave the incumbent off their ballots entirely, could the maneuver deprive him of votes he might otherwise receive.
 Alaska Republicans have a history of refusing to rank their choices, and the senator’s latest radio ad features a catchy jingle encouraging people to rank “Dan S., Daniel, Gerry, just don’t rank Mary.”
 “Republicans can be very stubborn,” Ms. Eledge said. “Some of them don’t like the system, so they don’t use it.”
 That approach could be even more consequential in the race for governor, also on this year’s ballot.
 A Democrat hasn’t won the job since 1998, but Democratic candidates finished first and second in the top-four August primary, which featured 17 candidates — 12 of them Republicans.
 The second-place Democrat dropped out to clear a path for the other, a former state legislator, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins . The top Republican finisher, Bernadette Wilson, urged the other two Republicans on the November ballot to do the same, but they refused. Earlier this month, President Trump backed Ms. Wilson and called on the other two Republicans to leave the race.
 It all has some conservatives worried their voters will ignore repeated party instructions to “rank the red” and instead list only one candidate.
 A similar approach helped Ms. Peltola defeat two Republicans, Sarah Palin and Nick Begich III, in a 2022 U.S. House race. The combined first-choice vote share for the two Republicans exceeded Ms. Peltola’s. But about a fifth of Mr. Begich’s voters only ranked him. When he fell out of the race, Ms. Peltola expanded her lead to win.
 Polls have shown Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins leading the governors race, and he has promised to build a politically balanced cabinet and work closely with Republicans and independents in the legislature, which has been governed by a bipartisan coalition.
 Proponents of the current system say its repeal could make such cooperation more difficult, by bringing back partisan primaries, which favor the extremes in both parties and gives Republican and Democratic leaders far more power to keep members focused on the party line.
 That’s exactly what Ms. Eledge and other opponents of the current system want.
 She’s eager, for example, to punish Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican, for her recent cross-party endorsement of Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins.
 If Ballot Measure 2 passes, Ms. Eledge predicted, “she won’t run again.”
 She added, “she knows she wouldn’t make it out of the primary.”
 Of course, Ms. Murkowski could do what she did in 2010 when she lost the Republican primary to a hard-line conservative: launch a successful write-in campaign , without ranked-choice.

 Andrew Duehren covers tax policy in Washington, and Laurel Rosenhall writes about California politics and policy.
 The prospects for a national wealth tax are on the ballot in California. 
 Image Credit... Mike Kai Chen for The New York Times For the architects of the novel billionaire tax on the ballot in California this week, the strategy was supposed to be relatively straightforward.
 First, harness widespread frustration with wealth inequality to pass what supporters believed would be an overwhelmingly popular ballot initiative. Then use California as an example to the country that a tax on wealth could work, propelling the idea further into the mainstream and eventually into federal law.
 That vision could still come to at least partial fruition if Proposition 40 passes. But the path through California to a federal wealth tax, a progressive dream for years, now looks like it could be a circuitous one, if not a dead end.
 Polls have shown limited support for Proposition 40, which would charge a one-time, 5 percent tax on the wealth of Californians worth more than $1.1 billion. Some recent surveys suggest the ballot measure may even fail. Billionaires have blanketed California’s airwaves with ads claiming that the tax could expand to apply to everyone.
 Democrats and labor unions, meanwhile, are divided over the tax. Groups representing teachers, doctors and firefighters warn that Proposition 40 could wind up harming the state budget in the long run if it drives entrepreneurs away from California. Many Democrats across the country have kept their distance from the proposal, as they assess its popularity and the potential problems with a federal version of a wealth tax.
 However the Nov. 3 vote turns out, the proponents and opponents of the billionaire tax agree that its importance goes well beyond California. At stake is a potential revolution in U.S. taxation. The once-radical concept of taxing wealth may soon gain a foothold in the nation’s most populous state. Or it may be dealt a surprising setback in a popular vote, puncturing the hope that such a policy would draw broad support.
 Image Mr. Sanders was joined by Jane Kim and Randy Villegas during a stop on his ‘Fighting Oligarchy: Where We Go From Here’ tour in Bakersfield, Calif. on Oct. 4, 2026. Credit... Kyle Grillot for The New York Times “The whole country is watching what you are doing here,” Senator Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent, told a crowd of supporters in California last month.
 For decades, the United States has relied on taxes on income — largely the wages people earn working — to fund federal and state governments. Money made on stocks, bonds and other holdings is generally only taxed when the assets are sold, and the paper gains become cash income. But as the nation’s richest people have seen the value of their financial portfolios soar, progressive policymakers have sought to tax their assets before they are sold, by creating a wealth tax.
 During the last competitive Democratic presidential primary, in 2020, progressive candidates such as Mr. Sanders and Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, made wealth taxes a central part of their platforms. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. eventually endorsed a plan, called the billionaire minimum income tax , that would have taxed unrealized gains, a form of wealth taxation. Donors to Vice President Kamala Harris’s campaign pushed her to drop the Biden plan once she took over the Democratic ticket in 2024.
 Passage of Proposition 40 in California, especially by a healthy margin, could make the idea of a wealth tax more palatable to Democrats who run in the party’s next presidential primary. Some progressive candidates are likely to adopt a wealth tax as part of their platform in any case. But a strong showing for the idea in California could convince others to put a version of the idea on their agendas.
 A loss or even a narrow victory could have the opposite effect. An internal document from a group opposing the tax said it seeks to “chill wealth tax efforts nationally” by defeating Proposition 40, according to previous reporting by The New York Times. 
 Some potential Democratic presidential candidates have already taken a stance on Proposition 40, including Representative Ro Khanna of California, who has campaigned in favor of the tax, and Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, who has opposed it. Mr. Newsom has said he supports raising other taxes on billionaires at the federal level.
 Image Mr. Newsom opposes the tax. Credit... Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times “If Prop. 40 goes down in California, I think it’s going to make, not all of the candidates, but it’s going to make a few of the 2028 candidates rethink how they slot that into their presidential policy agenda,” said Zach Moller, the senior director of the economic program at Third Way, a center-left think tank. “If it goes the other way, maybe that makes it seem like it’s a better idea.”
 A wealth tax would be a fundamental change in the tax system, raising complicated questions for tax collectors. That includes how to value holdings, like privately owned businesses, that may not have an existing price. Even for billionaires who derive their wealth from the publicly traded stocks of companies they founded, collecting the tax could be complicated if they do not have enough cash to pay it without selling many of their holdings.
 The economists and tax lawyers who crafted the California billionaire tax believe that their design has resolved those issues, creating a blueprint for federal and other state policymakers.
 “If California enacts a wealth tax, it will begin raising substantial revenues by 2027, and by 2028 we will have actual numbers and data and experience,” said David Gamage, a tax law professor at the University of Missouri who helped draft the tax. “And it will be a lot harder for the opposition to make all these absurd claims, because there will be real experience on the ground we can look to.”
 But there are several key differences between the California billionaire tax and what a federal wealth tax could look like. Proposition 40 is a one-time tax, while a federal version would likely be an annual levy. Then there is the fact that much of the revenue from the California billionaire tax would be dedicated to backfilling cuts to the state’s Medicaid program, a consequence of a law President Trump signed last year.
 Funneling the receipts from the billionaire tax toward a specific purpose, rather than feeding them into the overall budget like a federal wealth tax likely would, has fractured the idea’s support in California. Some unions have objected to the fact that the tax would not help with the state’s other funding needs. And the head of the health care workers union that sponsored the ballot initiative, Dave Regan, is a polarizing figure in California politics.
 Image Lee Haywood handed out flyers while campaigning for Propoisition 40 in Berkeley, Calif., in October. Credit... Minh Connors for The New York Times As a result, some progressives in Washington appear to be hedging their bets about the outcome of the referendum. Opponents of the tax have also put other initiatives on the ballot that could cancel out Proposition 40 even if it passes, further scrambling the potential meaning of the results next week.
 “The unique nature of this tax design, the unique nature of California—I don’t know how much people in other states or at the federal level will glean from the outcome here, either for good or bad,” said Bharat Ramamurti, who worked in Mr. Biden’s White House and is a former aide to Ms. Warren.
 The California plan and a potential federal wealth tax also differ in how easy they would be to avoid — and how susceptible they are to legal challenges.
 State-level taxes are comparatively easy to escape by moving to another state, while a federal wealth tax could apply to U.S. citizens even if they leave the United States. Several high-profile billionaires, including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, took steps to leave California before the tax’s residency deadline at the start of the year. Those departures could reduce the revenue collected by the tax, as well as leave California without the income taxes that the departed billionaires would have paid the state over time.
 Josh Rauh, an economist at Stanford’s Graduate School of Business, has estimated that the billionaire tax could end up costing California more money than it generates. Mr. Rauh, who opposes Proposition 40, said in an interview that he thinks the flight of billionaires, as well as the possible legal challenges to the tax, would ultimately set a bad precedent for wealth taxation, if it passes.
 “I don’t think it’s going to be as easy as proponents might think to put in a wealth tax and collect the wealth,” he said.
 A federal wealth tax, while not facing the same challenge of potential tax flight, would come with an arguably more serious risk of legal challenges. Progressives and other liberal tax experts worry that the current, conservative-led Supreme Court would rule that a federal wealth tax is an unconstitutional “direct tax.” Those concerns have only grown more acute after several Biden initiatives, including the cancellation of student debt , were thrown out by the Supreme Court. Some, like Mr. Gamage, still believe a wealth tax would be constitutional.
 Whether it’s through a wealth tax or another mechanism, Democrats in California and on the presidential campaign trail will keep trying to raise taxes on the rich. Lorena Gonzalez, who leads the California Federation of Labor Unions, said the campaign in California had brought attention to the concentration of wealth and power among billionaires, setting the stage for more proposals to address the stratification of the economy.
 “I mean, shoot, put a bigger tax on yachts,” she said. “The point is: Should we tax billionaires? Should we do some massive taxes on billionaires to unrig the economy? Ultimately that’s not going to stop with this vote.”

 New Hampshire’s G.O.P. Senate candidate tries to keep Trump at arm’s length. 
 Image John E. Sununu, the Republican nominee for Senate in New Hampshire, greeted voters at an Oktoberfest celebration in Loudon, N.H. Credit... Sophie Park/Getty Images Debra Smith arrived at a recent candidates forum hating John E. Sununu, the Republican nominee for Senate in New Hampshire.
 Here, she thought, was another career politician — a former congressman and one-term senator seeking to reclaim his seat nearly 20 years after he lost it, riding the coattails of his father and his brother, both former governors of the state.
 A funny thing happened, though, as Mr. Sununu took questions about health care, housing and transportation policy from Chamber of Commerce types as they picked at caprese sandwiches. Ms. Smith found herself impressed as Mr. Sununu wove facts and experience into his answers, lifting the energy of the room.
 “He’s very substantial,” she said.
 But before Mr. Sununu left the function room at the Atlantic Grill in Rye, N.H., Ms. Smith, an independent voter, told him she still couldn’t vote for him.
 “Because of Trump, I can’t,” she said. “I told him I can’t take the risk.”
 Mr. Sununu, 62, has turned his comeback Senate campaign into a test of a tricky premise: that in 2026, it is possible to be both a Republican and independent of President Trump. Selling this idea is critical for any hope of success in a purple state that has never really warmed to the president. And as he trails Representative Chris Pappas, a Democrat, in the polls, he’s running out of time to convince the Debra Smiths of the world to buy it, particularly in a race that is considered critical to determining the balance of power in the Senate.
 Image Mr. Sununu, right, debating the Democratic nominee, Chris Pappas, last week in Manchester, N.H. Credit... Reba Saldanha/Associated Press He is trying. He once wrote an opinion essay that carried the headline “Trump is a loser.” He has insisted in a television ad that he has never even met the president. He rattles off a laundry list of their policy differences to anyone who will listen. And, perhaps more than any other Republican running for Senate right now, he has asked voters to do something that strains the American political imagination: Consider what happens after Mr. Trump.
 “In two years, the president will leave office,” he said on a debate stage last month. “And my question is, where do we go next?”
 The unsaid part of his bet is that, deep down, voters want a political future that looks like the past.
 A New Hampshire dynasty 
 New Hampshire Republicans have lost every race for the House and the Senate since the dawn of the Trump era, often by quite a lot, even as they have won office at the state level. But the party saw a ray of hope in the Sununu name, which is synonymous with the flinty, establishment Republicanism that used to be a lot more common in New England. Mr. Sununu’s father, John H. Sununu, served as governor for three two-year terms in the 1980s before serving as chief of staff to President George H.W. Bush.
 National Republicans had tried unsuccessfully to convince Chris Sununu, Mr. Sununu’s charismatic younger brother and a former governor, to run for the Senate in 2022 against the incumbent Democrat, Maggie Hassan. By early 2025, they were seeking to lure John E. Sununu into the 2026 race. But when Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the longtime Democratic incumbent, announced she would retire, Chris Sununu coyly hinted he might run for the Senate after all. A person familiar with the recruiting efforts said that national Republicans checked in to gauge how serious he was — nobody wanted two Sununus on the ballot, after all — but Chris ultimately demurred.
 Image Signs in support of Mr. Sununu’s campaign being set up recently in Hampton Falls, N.H. Credit... Sophie Park/Getty Images Today, the campaign signs dotting the state’s landscape read, simply, “Sununu Senator,” without specifying which one is actually running. Democrats have conducted private polling to see if voters know which family member is on the ballot. They say confusion abounds.
 One reporter’s text message meant for John E. Sununu recently made it, instead, to his father.
 “You have reached the old ancient former Gov. of New Hampshire,” came the reply, which concluded, “not the young dynamic Sen.”
 The current candidate says there is no confusion. “Voters absolutely know who I am,” he said.
 Mr. Sununu first ran for Congress 30 years ago and held the seat currently occupied by Mr. Pappas for three terms. He won his Senate seat in 2002, in a strong year for Republicans in the wake of Sept. 11, and lost it to Ms. Shaheen in the wave that accompanied the election of Barack Obama in 2008. (He then pursued a lucrative career working at a lobbying firm and sitting on corporate boards.)
 Image Mr. Sununu, campaigning for Congress in 1996, chats with his wife, Catherine, and former President George H.W. Bush in Rye, N.H. Credit... Marcia Curtis/Associated Press On the campaign trail, he tells war stories from another era. He can be trusted to stand up to Mr. Trump, he says, because he stood up to President George W. Bush, insisting that the reauthorization of the Patriot Act, passed after the Sept. 11 attacks, include more protections for civil liberties. He can be trusted to be bipartisan, he says, because he cosponsored legislation with Hillary Clinton. He was the first Republican to call for the firing of Alberto Gonzales, the attorney general for Mr. Bush. (Mr. Gonzales resigned in 2007 after a standoff with congressional critics over the Justice Department’s handling of terrorism investigations and the firing of U.S. attorneys.)
 “I think all of those things reinforce a reputation for independence and for directness and honesty,” he said in an interview.
 And did his family name help?
 “Sure,” he said, quickly changing the subject to how, in 2024, he endorsed former Gov. Nikki Haley of South Carolina for president over Mr. Trump.
 Endorsed by the president 
 In February, Mr. Trump endorsed Mr. Sununu, saying he would work “tirelessly to advance our America first agenda.”
 It was a signal to the party to ignore Mr. Sununu’s primary opponent, another former Republican senator named Scott Brown . But it gave Mr. Pappas his biggest attack line: that, for all his claims of independence, Mr. Sununu is as beholden to Mr. Trump as anyone in a Republican Party that has shown total fealty to the president. Mr. Pappas has also depicted him as squishy on Mr. Trump, saying that Mr. Sununu’s opposition to the war in Iran, for instance, has bloomed only alongside its unpopularity.
 Mr. Sununu has tried to keep his focus on his state.
 Image Mr. Sununu greeting a supporter at his primary night watch party in September. Credit... CJ Gunther/Getty Images “My focus has been on New Hampshire, on the economy, jobs, affordability, and that message has resonated, and that’s why this is a race that a year ago people didn’t think would be competitive,” Mr. Sununu said.
 A New York Times/Siena University poll released in late September found Mr. Pappas with a five-point lead — a sign that Mr. Sununu is running significantly more competitively than the state’s last two Republican Senate nominees. One of them, Corky Messner, lost to Ms. Shaheen by nearly 16 percentage points in 2020; the other, Don Bolduc, lost to Senator Maggie Hassan by 9 points. (In a twist, Mr. Bolduc has endorsed Mr. Pappas.)
 In that poll, Mr. Sununu’s favorability rating was slightly higher than Mr. Pappas’s, at 45 percent to 43 percent. And 48 percent of voters said Mr. Sununu would better handle issues related to the cost of living; 46 percent said that about Mr. Pappas.
 But 60 percent of voters disapproved of Mr. Trump, and 54 percent said they wanted a candidate who would provide a check on him.
 ‘Existential threat’ 
 As he spoke to the Seacoast Chamber Alliance late last month, Mr. Sununu seemed, at times, to be inhabiting a kind of Brigadoon where there was no President Trump.
 He called for term limits in Congress, lamented the unbalanced state of the federal budget and eagerly parried questions about Social Security, going deep into the weeds.
 Mr. Pappas had addressed the group first. When he finished, Jimmy Dykes, an independent voter from the coastal town of Hampton, asked why the congressman had not been more visible in that community. But Mr. Dykes said he was planning to vote for Mr. Pappas, anyway.
 Image Mr. Sununu has tried to keep his focus on New Hampshire. Credit... Amanda Sabga/Reuters He associated Mr. Sununu with the wars that began during his tenure in Congress, those in Iraq and Afghanistan, and said he simply couldn’t trust him to deal with Mr. Trump, who he believes is an “existential threat.”
 Mr. Dykes was, however, considering voting for Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who has also stayed well away from Mr. Trump. She used to have the job Mr. Sununu wants but narrowly lost re-election to the Senate the night Mr. Trump was elected in 2016. Now, she appears to be cruising to re-election as governor — becoming one of her party’s bright spots in a difficult year.
 Mr. Sununu, for his part, declined to say what he thought the Republican Party should look like after Mr. Trump is gone. But does he want to help shape it?
 “Absolutely.”
 Bayliss Wagner contributed reporting.

 Even as marketers shift their dollars toward other media, broadcast TV remains king. 
 In the tight Senate race between Ken Paxton, left, and James Talarico, $220 million has been spent on broadcast ads through Oct. 28, more than half of the total spending. Doug Mills/The New York Times, Antranik Tavitian for The New York Times The deluge of political advertising in this year’s midterm elections is shattering previous records.
 Almost half of that money is going to a surprising place: your local TV channel.
 Advertisers, following the changing viewing habits of Americans, have increasingly shifted their marketing dollars to social platforms, streaming channels and other digital media. Yet when it comes to federal and state races, politicians and PACs are brushing aside concerns that TV ads are costlier to produce and less efficient in targeting prospective voters — and are showering local stations with billions of dollars.
 This election will show how much that calculus still holds in a transformed media environment.
 “I think the Democrats and Republicans are both spending a disproportionate amount of their budgets on broadcast TV at this point,” said Danielle Butterfield, a Democratic strategist and the executive director of Priorities USA. “Because you can see so clearly what’s happening on the other side, there’s this muscle memory needing to chase and match.”
 Political consultants and television executives argue that while broadcast TV may not be what it once was, those ads can reach a larger swath of the population more quickly than through other media. And that audience watching their nightly news programs, not to mention their favorite sitcoms, dramas and football games, is a devoted one.
 “Local anchors and reporters are trusted, familiar voices,” said Gregg Siegel, senior vice president of national sales at Sinclair Broadcast Group, one of the country’s largest owners of local TV stations. “They don’t just cover the communities they serve. They live there, raise their families there and are part of the fabric of those communities. That connection creates a level of credibility that is difficult to replicate on other platforms.”
 The amount of money being spent on political advertising this election cycle is staggering, helping to boost the bottom lines of the biggest local broadcasting companies like Sinclair, Nexstar Media Group, Gray Media, Tegna and the E.W. Scripps Company.
 The research firm S&P Global projects broadcast television advertising this year to be 15 percent higher than the last nonpresidential election year in 2022. And political ad revenue alone is expected to account for 16.3 percent of total broadcast revenue for the year, which would be a record for a nonpresidential election year.
 During this election cycle, total political advertising is expected to reach $11.6 billion by Election Day, according to AdImpact; $5.6 billion (48 percent) is flowing to broadcast. That dollar figure is even higher than the one during the 2024 presidential race, when $5.3 billion was spent on broadcast advertising, still 48 percent of the total.
 That growth is an outlier in the overall advertising market, where TV’s share continues to shrink as do the overall dollars. In 2024, for example, TV made up 15 percent of all ad spending in the United States, according to the research firm eMarketer. This year, projections envision that figure to be 10 percent.
 Nowhere is the broadcast TV blitz more evident than in Texas, where more than half a billion dollars will be spent in the Senate runoff, primaries and general election campaigns.
 Oscar Rodriguez, the president of the Texas Association of Broadcasters, said stations in all 20 media markets across the state were seeing ad buys, rather than just a few individual markets. “This is an election where clearly every single vote is going to matter,” he said.
 In the tight Senate race between Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate, and James Talarico, his Democratic opponent, $220 million had been spent on broadcast ads through Oct. 28, more than half of the total spending, according to AdImpact. The Paxton campaign and its Republican allies account for most of the broadcast TV outlays, and much of that has been supported by Elon Musk , the world’s richest man with deep business ties to Texas.
 Nick Maddux, a senior adviser to Mr. Paxton, said that it was most efficient for the campaign to spend money on linear television because of federal rules that ensure candidates (and at least for now, political parties and joint fund-raising committees ) get low-cost TV ad rates.
 The campaign’s statewide ad onslaught in October resulted in some ad breaks airing three Paxton spots for every one Talarico ad.
 “You go big and fast,” Mr. Maddux said.
 Luke Warford, a Democratic political consultant in Texas and chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party, said the Talarico campaign had focused more on building Mr. Talarico’s brand on social media. But the campaign and its Democratic allies have still spent heftily on broadcast TV, devoting 45 percent of their budgets to the medium through Oct. 28, according to AdImpact. (Republicans are at 60 percent.)
 Advertising on television can be a blunt force approach to reaching prospective voters, particularly in House races where viewers are often bombarded with ads for candidates in districts not their own. Danilo Yanich, a University of Delaware professor who runs the school’s Local Television News Project, said that’s a trade-off campaigns and PACs will take. “They’ll tolerate those inefficiencies because they’re not sure which voters they will not reach if they try to do those directed kinds of advertising campaigns.”
 “Local television viewers are very serious voters,” he added.
 And the people who watch broadcast television are often those who vote.
 “The kinds of people who tend to be very likely to vote in midterm elections tend to lean older,” Joshua Kalla, a professor of political science at Yale, said. “And those people still watch a whole bunch of broadcast TV.”
 There’s another incentive driving this advertising strategy: money. Consultants and media buying firms typically take up to a 15 percent commission on their ad buys, which, given some of the multimillion dollar spends, can quickly add up.
 Aaron Evans, a Republican campaign consultant, said that while broadcast had historically “been the beast that moves the numbers,” it was getting less effective every election cycle.
 “The thing that is making that industry really outlast its effectiveness is the fact it’s been a cash cow for these consulting firms for decades,” he said.
 Image Much of the ad spending for Mr. Paxton is supported by Elon Musk, the world’s richest man with deep business ties to Texas. Credit... Demetrius Freeman for The New York Times Some political operatives bemoan what they see as an outdated approach to advertising. During this year’s primaries, several candidates who were vastly outspent on TV ads still prevailed, including Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who triumphed over his Democratic rival, Haley Stevens, in Michigan.
 Ms. Butterfield, the Democratic strategist, pointed to internal research from Priorities USA that found that 83 percent of registered voters reported in using YouTube and 82 percent used streaming services in a single week in September, while just 61 percent said they watched linear TV. She said that ads on digital platforms, which were much cheaper than TV ads, could see a higher reach and have a more targeted impact.
 “The biggest difference between a broadcast television strategy and a digital strategy is how much the campaign actually uses the internet to not just broadcast and shout at a voter, but understand where that voter is, what they care about,” she said.
 Mr. Warford, the Democratic political consultant, said Tuesday’s vote would help answer a question about the broadcast television-heavy ad strategy in support of Mr. Paxton. “Is there an amount of money that can save an incredibly weak candidate in a tough environment at the end?”
